source.title: Taking Shortcuts for Categorical VQA Using Super Neurons
source.authors: Pierre Musacchio; Jae-Yong Jeong; Dahun Kim; Jaesik Park

record.tranche_reason: The paper studies scalar neuron activations as task-specific classifiers, but does not test whether neuron poles have one or more semantic jobs, whether explanations predict activation on held-out examples, or whether attribution graphs built from neurons explain model behaviour.
record.gate_note: The paper reports task-classification results from selected scalar activations. These do not measure the claim versions' semantic interpretability, explanation quality, or circuit-level explanation. Results cited from other work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study thresholds scalar activations (residual-stream dimensions, Layers × hidden dim) of VLMs and selects those that classify categorical VQA answers well. It never explains neurons, counts their jobs, scores explanations, or builds attribution graphs. Task-classification accuracy of selected scalars is a different construct from the claim's interpretability shares. Its cross-dataset overlap figure shows some scalars help on several tasks, but it does not interpret them. It neither tests nor relies on the claim, so T6.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors conclude that Super Neurons are strong, robust categorical classifiers that outperform or match the base models and sparse attention vectors, and that they enable extreme early exit with up to 5.10× speedup. Open-ended prompts and reasoning are left to future work.
record.recipe_differences: The paper thresholds raw neuron activations and selects them using task-specific probing-set performance to classify categorical VQA labels. It does not generate or test natural-language explanations of neuron jobs.
record.method_sensitivity: Results depend on dataset and the metric optimized during probing; the paper also varies probing-set size, activation threshold, token position, and aggregation method.

fits_no_version.finding: Thresholded single scalar activations in LLaVA and Qwen3-VL LLMs can classify categorical VQA answers at or above base-model performance, including in first-layer activations at the first generated token.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Individual VLM scalar activations can serve as task-specific categorical classifiers rivaling the full model.

fits_no_version.finding: Some selected scalars beat the model on several datasets at once, and one beats it on four (Supp. Fig. 2). The authors read this as neurons sharing expertise across tasks.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Some single activations carry task-relevant signal across multiple related VQA tasks.

record.problems: The reported results are task-specific classification scores and do not directly establish semantic interpretability or circuit explanations. No uncertainty estimates are reported.
record.rows_left_out: Many additional dataset, metric, aggregation, and model results appear in Tables 1–9 and supplementary tables. They are omitted because they report the same task-classification outcome rather than a distinct measurement relevant to the claim versions; the selected rows include the central Pope comparison, the stated Qwen occlusion weakness, and the scaled-up model result.

untested.parts: No audit of neuron poles or job counts in Qwen3-32B.
No interpretable-neuron shares in any model.
No test of architecture or tool effects on interpretability.
No neuron explanations tested on held-out text.

record.verdict_notes: The 'neurons' here are dimensions of layer activations (32×4096 for LLaVA), selected by task metric. This is not interpretation of MLP neurons. Rows are method-performance comparisons and are linked to no version.

versions.untested_parts: The paper does not audit neuron poles for one main job, related jobs, or unexplained cases.
The paper evaluates selected task-classifying activations in VLMs, not shares of interpretable neurons across dense and mixture-of-experts LLMs up to trillions of parameters.
No InceptionV1 cat-and-car example, shared pose feature, or recursive generalization is tested.
The paper does not test architecture, regularization, tool quality, or interpretability-share estimates for vision models.
The paper uses selected neuron activations as categorical classifiers; it does not build attribution graphs or test reconstruction error or circuit explanations.
The paper does not test explanations against held-out activating examples or measure whether they predict where neurons fire.
The paper does not score neuron explanations by simulating activations on new text.

rows.subject: LLaVA-v1.5-7b
rows.operation_detail: Selected scalar activations were thresholded and aggregated as task classifiers; validation performance reported for mean and majority voting.
rows.note: This is task-classification performance, not a measurement of semantic job count or explanation quality.
rows.check: Classification accuracy of selected scalars vs the base model's answer. This is the study's own method compared with the model, not a measure of neuron interpretability.
